cells.tense: You can touch one shared thing you carry and feel that it still fits, instead of weighing it constantly.
cells.ask: Name one shared thing you carry forward and one you have quietly stopped. Say the second part out loud, once.
cells.core: You know the difference between a thing worth carrying forward and a thing you keep from habit, and you can name it without making a production out of leaving. That's a harder skill than it sounds — most people either keep everything or drop everything at once. When a shared practice or phrase passes through you and fits, it stays alive rather than preserved under glass. The same ability runs when something has gone flat: you set it down without drama, and you don't need the people around you to agree before you do. What's already working is that you can tell the two apart in the moment, not years later. For a next small move, put one live thing and one spent thing in words in front of someone who shares them with you. Hearing yourself say which is which is what keeps this deliberate.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell what still carries, and set down what doesn't.
cells.verb: to test what still carries forward and step past what no longer does
cells.place: in whatever your people have always done together, where the meanings you share are kept and handed on

cells.tense: You are standing on the far shore of a shared thing before anyone has agreed to cross with you.
cells.ask: Pick one shared thing that's still working. Do it again the same way this week, no improvements, and notice what happens when nobody's watching.
cells.core: You've already decided which of your shared things is finished, and you're acting like the goodbye has been said. In practice people are still holding the old form, still expecting it, and you've moved on ahead of them — so a lot of your conversations carry a tug you don't state out loud. The leaving itself may be right. Doing it at speed and alone is what costs you: the shared meaning only thins out cleanly if the people who kept it can see you go. There's another way this can go — you spot the thing that's outlived its use and you end it, and the room feels relieved because you said so first. Look at where you've been treating it as over before it's over. That's a different decision than whether to leave.
cells.sheetLine: You've left in your head before anyone else has left the room.
cells.verb: to test what still carries forward and step past what no longer does
cells.place: in whatever your people have always done together, where the meanings you share are kept and handed on

cells.tense: A shared practice you used to stay inside has been behind you for a while, and you haven't put a word on it.
cells.ask: Say one half-formed thought about what you share with these people out loud to one of them, wrong wording allowed, before it's polished.
cells.core: Something you used to do with your people stopped, and rather than say it ended you just stopped showing up for it. From outside it looks like nothing changed, which is how you've been keeping it. The trouble isn't the leaving — it's that nothing new has come up where the old thing was. So the shared things you do now are the ones other people bring, and your own contributions have gone quiet. That's not a problem in the group. It's one way of taking part in you, thinly supplied, and it pulls from the same thinking that used to be yours — noticing the shape of things, saying what you notice. Send one honest, unfinished observation to one person who shares this with you. It doesn't need to be right. It needs to have left your head.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped showing up and didn't say anything out loud.
cells.verb: to test what still carries forward and step past what no longer does
cells.place: in whatever your people have always done together, where the meanings you share are kept and handed on

cells.tense: You are already changing what your people carry forward, and you keep describing it as just what's happening.
cells.ask: Name one change you've made in a shared practice as yours — to one person, in a sentence that starts with 'I decided'.
cells.core: You've been deciding what survives and what doesn't — which words still get used, which old routines have quietly stopped, which things get repeated because you repeat them. That's your hand on it, and you're doing it well enough that nobody's noticed, including you. It gets filed under 'that's just how it went' or 'we all agreed', and the credit goes nowhere. What's already working is the taste: you drop the stale parts and keep the live ones, and the group follows. What's missing is that you don't claim it, so when someone pushes back you have no position to stand on. Say the decision as a decision, out loud, to one person who shares this. Not for credit — so that when it's questioned, there's a place you made it from.
cells.sheetLine: You're already changing what gets carried. You just won't say it's you.
cells.verb: to test what still carries forward and step past what no longer does
